source.title: How Far Do Simple Transformations Translate Across Text Embedding Models?
source.authors: Sid Ali Hamideche; Louis-Adrien Dufrène; Quentin Lampin; Guillaume Larue

record.file_problem: The paper text is present through its appendices. Some figures and matrix layouts are flattened, but the text explicitly describes their main patterns.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether simple mappings and measured representational similarity generalize across heterogeneous text embedding models; reports structured successes and failures that qualify broad universality claims.
record.gate_note: The study measures cross-model geometry, translation fidelity, retrieval, and downstream transfer. It does not sweep model scale or capability, compare independently trained seeds, test image-caption pairs, or identify recurring features. Cited findings from other papers are not recorded as results. The paper reports that anchor-set choice did not produce a consistent performance difference; this is included as a result. Large figure matrices are not transcribed cell by cell where their layout is flattened; the paper's explicit descriptions of those results are recorded.
record.test_reason: The study measures how well simple translators (Linear pinv, relative representations, IRP, Linear SGD) map nine heterogeneous text-embedding models onto each other, using CKA, transfer, fidelity and retrieval. Its results directly test V4 and V7, and in a limited way V6 (anchor set and diagnostic choice). The authors explicitly argue that universality up to a simple map fails for many pairs. It runs no scale sweep, no seeds, no image-text pairs and no feature analysis.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that simple, mostly linear, translators work only for some compatible pairs that share architecture family, objective, pooling and data. Many pairs degrade sharply, and failures are structured: whole class boundaries collapse. This pushes back against strong universality claims, including the Platonic hypothesis, for heterogeneous text embeddings. They also say universality is 'not completely untrue', given Linear (SGD)'s results, and that nonlinear translators may close more of the gap.
record.recipe_differences: Tests cross-model alignment and transfer using CKA, linear maps, relative representations, inverse relative projection, fidelity, classification, and retrieval on nine text embedding models. This is not a scale sweep or a replication of the original Platonic cross-modal scale analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model pair, downstream task, translation method, and diagnostic. The study reports no consistent difference between its two anchor sets.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix A: analogy decompositions (king ≈ α·queen + β·man + γ·woman) give the same sign pattern in all nine models. Coefficients become unstable with a 14-concept basis, especially for unnormalised models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Low-dimensional local semantic linear structure is shared across heterogeneous encoders even when global maps fail.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix D: models with high hubness (e5-large-v2, Qwen3) perform poorly as k-NN retrieval targets; Qwen3 nonetheless does well as a source.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hubness of the target space limits retrieval-based measures of cross-model alignment.

record.problems: The authors report no uncertainty estimates or compute accounting. The evaluation uses a finite model set and classification-oriented tasks, and its fixed SVM setup may understate absolute performance. It evaluates pooled fixed-length embeddings rather than sequence-level representations. Some pairwise figure matrices are difficult to recover from the flattened text.
record.rows_left_out: Pair-by-pair cells from the downstream accuracy matrices in Figures 2 and 11-16, the pairwise entries of the fidelity and retrieval matrices in Figures 3-4 and 8-10, and hubness tables 3-5 are not separately transcribed; their layouts are flattened and the paper's explicit aggregate or qualitative findings are recorded instead. Table 2's reported task-by-method aggregates are all included.

untested.parts: No sweep over model size or capability. The largest model (Qwen3-4B) is only moderately compatible, but this is not a scale test.
Untested: stitching layers, nonlinear maps, unpaired (unsupervised) alignment, and token-level or sequence representations.
No feature, neuron, SAE or circuit analysis.
Untested: out-of-distribution inputs, CKA variants or kernel settings, and a systematic sweep of k or neighbourhood size for mutual-kNN-style metrics.
Plateauing with scale is untested. Shared data or objectives are not isolated experimentally; the causal attributions are post hoc.

missing.what: Pair-level values for e5-large-v2 as source or target. Examples: RR DBpedia transfer ≈0.07 (chance); RR top-1 retrieval from e5 ≈0.00–0.01; pinv top-1 ≈0.02–0.05. Needed to ground the V4 challenge for that model.
Pair-level values for the gtr-t5-large/instructor-xl pair, e.g. pinv DBpedia transfer 0.92/0.88 and RR retrieval top-1 1.00, showing near-complete interchangeability for the best pair.
The full CKA matrix: off-diagonal non-e5 values range about 0.54–0.66; e5 pairs 0.25–0.27.

Linear (SGD) retrieval with sentence anchors, which is much higher (many pairs above 0.8 at top-10), against RR and pinv. This shows strong dependence of measured interchangeability on the translator.
Mean cosine and normalised error after translation per pair, for pinv and SGD (e.g., e5-sourced pinv normalised error of 2.7–4.3).

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Measured interchangeability depends strongly on the translator: on DBpedia, RR gives 17.62 and Linear SGD 89.11 (r18 vs r20). This bears on V6 only if translators count as measures, so the rows are kept under V4. Same-model references use the lossy T_i→i translation, not raw embeddings. MRPC, and to a lesser extent QQP and CoLA, have near-chance references, which weakens those rows. Results come from single runs with no uncertainty reported, and from a fixed RBF-SVM. The study cites the Platonic hypothesis but does not test scale, so it does not bear on V1.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size or capability sweep; no test of whether alignment rises with scale or performance.
No vision-language model pair or paired image-caption representations.
No same-architecture models trained from different initializations, or shared-feature/subspace analysis.

Tests fixed-length word and sentence embeddings with simple mappings; does not test stitching layers, token-level sequence representations, relative representations without paired inputs, or nonlinear mappings.
No analysis of recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits.
Tests several diagnostics, anchor/input sets, and retrieval k values, but not a systematic sweep of metric settings or out-of-distribution inputs.

Finds incomplete, pair-dependent transfer and discusses training/design similarities as explanations; does not isolate shared data or objectives experimentally from other model differences, and does not test plateauing with scale.

rows.subject: gtr-t5-large and instructor-xl
rows.operation_detail: Linear CKA between embeddings of shared anchors
rows.note: The paper calls this the most similar pair, but describes the overall pattern as structured and non-uniform.
rows.check: CKA is a similarity score, not a mapping, so it does not bear on V4; it bears on V6 only if paired with a metric comparison. The value 0.81 is the highest off-diagonal CKA in Figure 1; most other pairs fall at 0.54–0.66. It bears on V7 (incomplete alignment).

rows.subject: e5-large-v2 and Qwen3-Embedding-4B
rows.operation_detail: Linear CKA between embeddings of shared anchors
rows.note: The paper identifies e5-large-v2 as a pronounced outlier; the matrix reports this pair's CKA as 0.26.
rows.check: CKA, not a mapping, so it does not bear on V4. CKA is about 0.25–0.27 for every e5-large-v2 pair, not just this one. The authors partly attribute this to e5's narrow cosine range affecting angle-sensitive metrics, but e5 also fails in transfer and retrieval.

rows.subject: Nine-model collection
rows.operation_detail: Compared anchor-based translators using the Basic English word list and Wikitext-103 sentence anchors

conditions.value: 850 Basic English words versus 850 Wikitext-103 sentences

rows.value: The authors report no consistent performance difference between the two anchor sets.
rows.note: The authors also report no significant gains from more elaborate anchor selection; this is a qualitative result, not a quantified comparison.
rows.check: This is a methodological statement (no consistent difference between Basic English and Wikitext anchors) with no numbers. It bears on V6's input dependence, not V4. The authors also attribute IRP's advantage to anchor pruning and admit they did not push anchor selection far.

rows.subject: Nine-model collection
rows.operation_detail: Compared bidirectional cross-model classification-transfer compatibility across model pairs and methods

conditions.value: Nine text embedding models with differing architecture, training objective, pooling, normalization, and data

rows.measure: Cross-model transfer accuracy; symmetric compatibility averaged over directions, methods, and tasks
rows.baseline: Same-model transfer is higher on average; exact aggregate compatibility value not stated.
rows.value: Compatibility varies by pair and task; gtr-t5-large/instructor-xl transfer well bidirectionally, e5-large-v2 is consistently a poor source and target, and Qwen3-Embedding-4B has moderate compatibility.
rows.note: The authors describe non-uniform, structured pairwise transfer, with the most compatible pairs associated with shared architectural and training choices.
rows.check: Not linked to V6 but was listed in the V6 label; remove it from that label. e5-large-v2 pairs are near chance in several matrices (e.g., RR on DBpedia ≈0.07), which this row summarises only qualitatively.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.2, pairwise-transfer discussion; Section 6, symmetric compatibility definition and model-cluster discussion.

relationships.condition: Compatible pairs (gtr-t5-large/instructor-xl) and the learned Linear (SGD) map on AG News, DBpedia and SST-2
relationships.reason: Linear SGD keeps most same-model accuracy (DBpedia 89.11 vs 96.97; AG News 83.48 vs 89.63; SST-2 84.97 vs 90.92), and the T5 pair transfers well in both directions (r04, r08, r20, r36, r38).
relationships.display_finding: Mapped accuracies were 89.11 versus 96.97 on DBpedia, 83.48 versus 89.63 on AG News, and 84.97 versus 90.92 on SST-2, with good bidirectional transfer for the T5 pair.

source_check.condition: Compatible pairs (gtr-t5-large/instructor-xl) and the learned Linear (SGD) map on AG News, DBpedia and SST-2
source_check.reason: The T5 pair transfers well bidirectionally, and the stated SGD accuracies and same-model references match Table 2. These results support useful simple mappings in these conditions.

relationships.condition: Anchor-based translators (pinv, RR, IRP) across heterogeneous pairs, and harder tasks (emotion, QQP, CoLA) even with Linear SGD
relationships.reason: Cross-model averages fall far below same-model ones, e.g. RR on DBpedia 17.62 vs 73.51 and pinv on AG News 52.45 vs 85.15; even SGD on emotion gives 43.74 vs 59.72 (r01–r24, r29–r32, r37).
relationships.display_finding: Cross-model scores fell below same-model scores: ridge regression reached 17.62 versus 73.51 on DBpedia, pseudoinverse mapping 52.45 versus 85.15 on AG News, and linear SGD 43.74 versus 59.72 on emotion.

relationships.reason: The text says e5 is consistently a poor source and target, with low fidelity and outlier retrieval (r36, r37, r38). Figures show near-chance transfer and near-zero RR retrieval, which no row records, so this verdict rests partly on the text.
relationships.display_finding: Mappings involving e5-large-v2 showed low fidelity, near-chance transfer, and near-zero RR retrieval.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.reason: Section 5.2 explicitly identifies e5-large-v2 as a consistently poor source and target; Sections 5.3–5.4 report low fidelity and degraded retrieval. Chance-level transfer in several matrices contradicts low-loss interchangeability for these pairs.

relationships.condition: Anchor-set choice (Basic English words vs Wikitext sentences) and diagnostic choice (CKA, fidelity, retrieval, transfer)
relationships.reason: The anchor set made no consistent difference (r35). Retrieval broadly echoes transfer, though not always, and k-NN is affected by hubness (r37). Measured compatibility here is fairly robust to these choices.
relationships.display_finding: Anchor-set choice produced no consistent performance difference, while retrieval broadly tracked transfer with occasional disagreements and k-NN sensitivity to hubness.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Anchor-set choice (Basic English words vs Wikitext sentences) and diagnostic choice (CKA, fidelity, retrieval, transfer)
source_check.reason: For the anchor comparison in r35, Section 3 reports no consistent performance difference: the predicted input dependence is absent, warranting challenges for that narrow condition. Split off diagnostic choice: r37 reports retrieval/transfer disagreements and hubness sensitivity, supporting metric dependence rather than establishing uniform robustness.

relationships.reason: Most CKA values sit at 0.25–0.66, with a maximum of 0.81 (r33, r34), and cross-model transfer stays below same-model (r01–r24, r29–r32). The authors attribute the compatible clusters to shared backbone, pooling and contrastive training (r38).
relationships.display_finding: Most CKA values were 0.25–0.66, peaking at 0.81, and cross-model transfer underperformed same-model transfer; authors attributed compatible clusters to shared backbones, pooling and contrastive training.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: Figure 1 shows incomplete alignment, Table 2 shows transfer losses, and Sections 6 and 9 attribute compatible clusters to shared architectural and training choices. This supports partial convergence and the proposed alternative explanation, without a controlled causal test.
